title: The Fruit No One Had Ever Eaten
story:
The cowherd boys of Vrindavan had been out since morning with their calves, and the afternoon had settled into the slow, warm rhythm they knew well — the calves grazing, the boys at their games in the shade, the sun high and steady. It was an ordinary day, and it would have stayed an ordinary day, but for the wind. When it turned, it carried a scent they knew at once, and it stopped them in the middle of their play. The calves went on grazing, but the boys stood still, lifting their heads like animals catching a trail. Sweet, heavy, faint as a half-remembered dream, the smell drifted from the edge of the forest — from the one place in all their world that no one ever entered.

A little way off stood the palm grove, the talavana. In every season its trees let fall fruit so ripe and fragrant that the smell of it perfumed the air for a long way around. The verses say the fruit kept falling and lay fallen in such plenty that no one could ever have gathered it all — it never stopped coming. Yet it lay where it dropped, season after season, untouched. The ground beneath the palms was soft with over-ripe fruit, and no hand had ever gathered a single piece. No one in Vrindavan had ever tasted it.

The reason was no secret. The grove belonged to a demon named Dhenuka, who wore the form of a donkey, and his kin lived there with him, as fierce as he. He was enormously strong, and he had made men his food, and so the people of Vrindavan kept their distance. Even the grown men, who grazed their herds across every other corner of the forest, gave the grove a wide berth and would not walk past it alone. The fruit ripened and fell and rotted where it lay, and the boys could only look at it from far off, while the fragrance drifted over them and teased them.

That day the longing grew too strong to bear. The smell came again, sweet and insistent, and the boys could not turn away from it. They came running to Krishna and his elder brother Balarama, their words tumbling over one another. "Rama! Rama, mighty-armed! Krishna, destroyer of the wicked!" they cried. They told of the grove where the fruit fell and fell and was never eaten, and of the fierce donkey who guarded it and had made men his food. Their minds were greedy with the fragrance. "Give us that fruit," they begged.

Krishna heard his friends out, and heard the longing in their voices. He did not need to be persuaded, and he did not stop to weigh the danger. When he heard their words, the old verses say, he wished only to do what would please them. So the two brothers set out for the palm grove, the boys following close behind, and the sweet smell of the forbidden fruit grew stronger with every step they took toward it.
reflection: The boys do not try to take the fruit themselves; they know exactly where strength and protection lie, and they ask for what they want with a trust so complete it is almost childlike. The fragrance stands in for every desire that is lovely and safe-looking but guarded by something no one has dared to face.
next_story_tease: But the guardian of the grove would not give up its fruit so easily.
hero_scene: The cowherd boys clustered around Krishna and Balarama at the edge of the palm grove, pointing toward palms heavy with ripe fruit, the sweet fragrance hanging in the warm air as the brothers set out toward the forbidden trees.
visual_elements: palm grove heavy with ripe fruit
fallen fruit scattered on the ground
Dhenuka the donkey-demon unseen at the grove's heart
